name: Total maxillary osteotomy
lead: Total maxillary osteotomy, usually performed as a Le Fort I osteotomy, is an orthognathic (jaw) operation in which the whole upper jaw is cut free from the skull base and moved to a new position, then fixed in place. In the medical literature it is used for conditions such as vertical maxillary excess (often called long face syndrome), open bite and under-grown upper jaws, for example in cleft lip and palate [1]. In looksmaxxing culture it is classed as a hardmaxxing procedure, meaning a bone-level surgical change to facial structure.

Published research on the operation is mostly surgical: animal and cadaver studies of how the upper jaw keeps its blood supply after being cut, cephalometric (X-ray measurement) studies of skeletal change, and studies of related effects such as middle-ear function [2][3][4][5]. Registered trials focus on peri-operative questions such as anaesthesia, bleeding and pain control rather than on facial appearance outcomes [9][10][11].

Risks described in general references include bleeding, swelling, infection, nerve numbness and, rarely, permanent nerve injury; recovery involves weeks of healing and months of bone remodelling [1]. This is a major operation normally planned by surgeons together with orthodontists.

paras: The operation involves horizontal cuts through the maxilla, separation of the upper jaw from the cranial base and release of the pterygoid plates, after which the jaw is moved and secured. Surgeons use X-rays and planning to define the deformity beforehand and typically work with orthodontists who provide braces before and after surgery [1]. Care is taken to protect the descending palatine arteries and the blood supply to the segment [1].
The segment may be moved forward, upward (impaction) or downward, and in some techniques is divided into several pieces. Bone grafts may be placed in gaps created by movement [6][7][8].

General references list long face syndrome (vertical maxillary excess, hyperdivergent face), open bites, insufficient upper-jaw growth such as in cleft lip and palate, and some skeletal problems linked to sleep apnea or airway defects [1]. Orthognathic surgery of this kind is usually described as the main approach to correcting such skeletal discrepancies [1].

In looksmaxxing it is discussed as a way of repositioning of the whole upper jaw to address a long lower face. Enthusiasts group it with other hardmaxxing surgeries aimed at changing facial proportions. No studies in the material reviewed measure attractiveness or satisfaction after this operation specifically.

Initial healing is reported at roughly 2 to 6 weeks, with full bony union and remodelling taking a further 2 to 4 months. Jaws may be immobilised for 1 to 4 weeks in some protocols, patients commonly follow a liquid diet, and swelling may persist for months [1].

Reported complications include bleeding, swelling, infection, nausea and vomiting, and facial numbness from nerve injury that is usually temporary but can rarely be permanent. Infection rates of up to 7% are cited, with antibiotic prophylaxis used to reduce them, and maxillary impaction is described as riskier than some other jaw movements [1]. A study reported in the same overview found a high infection rate when third molars were removed during the osteotomy, which prompted caution about combining them [1].

Most published studies on total maxillary osteotomy are anatomical or animal research. A 1975 study in adult rhesus monkeys found minimal transient ischaemia, minimal bone death and early bone union, and that cutting the greater palatine arteries had no discernible effect on circulation to the teeth and bone [2]. A 1986 monkey study examined a technique that preserves two soft-tissue pedicles in a four-segment operation and its effects on revascularization and healing [4]. Studies in monkeys also looked at tooth pulp and root responses [7] and craniofacial adaptation [9].

In a cadaver study of ten specimens, the descending palatine arteries were interrupted by a Le Fort I osteotomy while the ascending palatine branch of the facial artery and a branch of the ascending pharyngeal artery remained in the attached palatal soft-tissue pedicle [3]. Human studies include a cephalometric study of changes during and after the Le Fort I procedure [5], studies of tympanometric (middle-ear) changes [10], and a study of middle-ear function and soft-palate muscle activity in cleft patients [11], as well as studies of healing of bone grafts placed during the operation [6][8].

Registered trials involve orthognathic surgery generally: a trial of ultrasound-guided suprazygomatic maxillary nerve block with bimaxillary osteotomy (completed, n=56) [12], a phase 4 trial of tranexamic acid for bleeding and swelling in orthognathic surgery (completed, n=104) [13], and a trial of local ketamine in orthognathic procedures (active, n=40) [14]. Results are not summarised here.

card.summary: Whole upper jaw cut and repositioned (Le Fort I) for long-face problems; a major, established jaw operation with solid surgical literature but little on looks outcomes.
card.aka: Le Fort I osteotomy; maxillary osteotomy
card.note: Major surgery under general anaesthesia; risks include infection, nerve numbness and bleeding.

quick.overview:
Total maxillary osteotomy moves the entire upper jaw, usually by a Le Fort I cut, to a new position. Medically it treats long face (vertical maxillary excess), open bite and under-grown upper jaws.

In looksmaxxing it is a hardmaxx option for changing facial proportions. Published work is mainly about surgical technique, healing and blood supply; no study in the reviewed material measures attractiveness outcomes.
quick.mechanism: Surgeons cut the maxilla horizontally, free it from the skull base, move it forward, up or down, and fix it, usually coordinated with orthodontic braces. Blood supply is preserved through the palatal soft tissue attached to the segment [3].
quick.risks: General references list bleeding, swelling, infection, nausea, and facial numbness that is usually temporary but can be permanent. Healing takes weeks, with months for bone remodelling, and it is a major operation requiring general or sedated care.
